## Part One:

The Laboratory  Chillwind 8, 963 BF, Approximately the Twelfth Hour

Waluigi must begin with the laboratory because the laboratory is where the context lives. You cannot understand what the expedition meant without understanding what the world looked like from inside the room where it started, and the room where it started tells you exactly what the Long Dark actually was when you were inside it rather than reading about it later from a distance of seventy-seven years.

Professor E. Gadd's laboratory in the Guild District was one of a very small number of scientific facilities still operating at meaningful capacity fourteen months into the infrastructure collapse. This is worth pausing on. Most research operations in the kingdom had scaled back or ceased entirely when Star Road power failed in 962 BF. The research that had driven the Mushroom Kingdom's scientific advancement for decades  the spectral studies, the magical engineering, the alchemical development  had stopped, not because researchers had stopped caring or funding had disappeared but because the energy source that ran the equipment simply did not exist anymore.

Laboratories full of sophisticated apparatus had become cold rooms full of expensive furniture.

The knowledge was still there.

The machines were still there.

The power to run them was not.

E. Gadd's laboratory ran on Guild emergency ration power. Approximately a third of normal operating capacity. This produced a specific set of conditions that Waluigi can reconstruct from the field notes and from descriptions provided by Long Dark survivors who worked in Guild-adjacent facilities during this period. The overhead lights flickered rather than burned steady  a rhythmic uncertain pulse that made shadows crawl across the workbenches in ways that seemed designed to unsettle visitors and that E. Gadd appeared genuinely not to notice. The temperature was marginal in the specific way of Long Dark heated spaces: warm enough to work, cold enough that you were always aware of the cold waiting at the edges, the kind of temperature that settled into joints and made fingers stiff and concentration brittle after extended periods.

The electric kettle had stopped working seven months prior when the power rationing dropped below its minimum wattage requirement.

Tea was brewed on a coal burner that E.

Gadd had installed himself, leaving soot marks on the ceiling above it that he had also not noticed or at least had not addressed.

The coal burner was a Long Dark adaptation  practical, functional, requiring no infrastructure beyond the coal itself.

E.

Gadd had made this adaptation so smoothly and so early that it appeared to have become part of the laboratory's permanent character rather than an emergency measure.

The laboratory was cluttered in the particular way of a workspace that has been both home and professional space for an extended period under conditions that do not permit the luxury of tidiness. Equipment piled on equipment across every horizontal surface. Poltergust components in various states of assembly and disassembly. Glass vials of substances arranged in rows that followed a logic visible only to E. Gadd and possibly not fully visible even to him. Papers covered in dense notation mixed with papers covered in sketches mixed with papers that appeared to be shopping lists for components that may or may not have been available for purchase in the current economy.

In one corner, a storage cabinet labeled TOP SECRET  DO NOT TOUCH UNLESS EXPERIENCED in large handwritten letters, which was the most organized thing in the room, which tells you something important about E.

Gadd's priority hierarchy: operational security received more attention than general organization.

Into this laboratory walked Leo. Waluigi does not have detailed documentation of Leo's arrival. The Guild record lists him as 'Trainee (Leo), assigned to Gadd Science emergency contract, Chillwind 963.' No prior service record. No background file beyond the assignment notation. No personal history visible in any document Waluigi has been able to access. He walked into E. Gadd's flickering coal-scented laboratory as a new trainee on his first field deployment during the worst infrastructure collapse in living memory, and the Guild record treats this as unremarkable enough to document in a single line.

Waluigi does not find it unremarkable.

Waluigi finds the gap between the single line and what actually happened during this departure sequence to be one of the most significant gaps in the available documentation of this period.

Luigi was already there when Leo arrived, mid-conversation with E. Gadd, handling Poltergust parts from his own standard-issue unit with the practiced ease of someone who has been working with the same equipment family for a very long time. The standard Poltergust  stable, reliable, built for containment rather than discovery  was Luigi's tool. He knew it completely. He had been using it, and tool

[... ADMINISTRATIVE PRUNING BY WALUIGI TO SAVE ARCHIVE SPACE ...]

nt, this profound ideological wound, was the armor Leo wore. It explains his coldness. It explains his fast processing speed and lack of panic. He was not waiting for a hero to save him, because he believed the hero had deserted them. He believed they were entirely on their own.They boarded the train.E. Gadd ushered them past the mechanical conductor droid, using the Clearance Token to secure access to what he called a 'strategically advantageous position.' This turned out to be a cramped, dirty, private observation nook tucked against a ventilation shaft in the very last car, partially obscured by a heavy velvet curtain.

The heavy pneumatic doors hissed shut, sealing them inside a vibrating, ozone-scented iron box.

The train lurched forward, plunging into the dark tunnels of the mountain pass.Luigi collapsed onto the stiff wooden bench.

He told Leo to focus on his breathing.

And then, Luigi did something that requires specific economic and psychological documentation: he reached into his pocket, pulled out a small, crumpled piece of hard candy with trembling fingers, and offered it to Leo.Sugar helps with the shock, Luigi said softly.

It helped Mario once.Waluigi wants to be extremely clear about what this gesture meant in 963 BF.

Sugar was not a casual commodity.

The agricultural supply chains that brought sugar cane to Toad Town had been severed for eight years by the civil war, and whatever reserves existed had been frozen or hoarded by the Mages Guild when the Star Road failed.

Sugar was pure, fast-burning calories.

In the Hoarfrost Winter of the Long Dark, calories were body heat.

Calories were literal survival.

For Luigi to give away a piece of sugar to a trainee he had met an hour ago was an act of profound, self-sacrificing generosity.

And he referenced Mario.

While Leo was silently despising Mario for running away, Luigi was invoking his brother's name as a comfort mechanism, passing on a lesson Mario had taught him.

The contrast between Leo's bitter resentment and Luigi's enduring, tragic devotion, occupying the exact same physical space on that train compartment, is the emotional core of this expedition.

Luigi still believed in the brother who had left him alone in a dying world.

Leo chewed the sugar.

As a reflex of a pre-collapse mindset, he began looking around the seat for a dinner menu.He did not find a menu.

He found a stiff piece of parchmenta topographical transit map of the rail line.

E.

Gadd snatched the map immediately, his magnifying glass hovering over the parchment.

He instantly identified operational hazards: Blackwood Pass, a deep subterranean trench marked with a skull-and-crossbones, notorious for signal interference.

If they lost contact with station HQ there, they would be flying blind through contested territory.

When Leo asked about the train's amenities, E.

Gadd laughed a harsh, wheezing laugh.

He pointed to the fine print on the map.

The Maglev Express did not serve dinner.

It featured an automated vending unit in the dining car that dispensed 'Nutrient Slurry' and dehydrated crackers.

Waluigi pauses on this detail.

The Mushroom Kingdom was once a civilization defined by its abundancefeasts, banquets, endless supplies of fresh food.

Now, its elite Mages Guild operatives, traveling on a high-security armored train to save a village from spectral annihilation, were expected to sustain themselves on heavily rationed, machine-dispensed sludge.

This was the texture of life in the second year of the Long Dark.Before the grim reality of the nutrient slurry could fully settle upon the group, the operational environment changed again, instantly and violently.A heavy, rhythmic *thud-thud-thud* sounded from the ceiling of the compartment.E.

Gadd froze.

The train was moving at tremendous speed through a subterranean mountain pass.

The sound was not the wind.

It was not a loose bolt.

It was the distinct, heavy sound of sharp, multi-jointed limbs scraping against the metal exterior of the train's roof.

E.

Gadd reached into his lab coat and retrieved a brass-encased ecto-meter.

He flicked it on.

The needle on the gauge violently slammed all the way to the right, pinning itself deep into the red zone.

A massive spectral density spike.

Directly above their heads.Stay low, E.

Gadd whispered, his face pale under the flickering compartment lamp, gripping Leo's sleeve.

If that pressure seal on the ceiling fails, we won't be worrying about dinner; we'll be worrying about whether our souls are still attached to our bodies!Waluigi's analysis of the departure phase concludes here.

The transit phase had officially begun.

They had successfully navigated the human threatsthe Guild checkpoints, the failing infrastructure, the security golems, and the crowded terminal.

But they were now moving through the Long Dark, trapped in a sealed iron box traveling at high speed, and the Long Dark had finally found them.

What follows on the roof of the Maglev Express is an entirely different operational paradigm.

description:
This filing belongs to the older haunted-estate era, not the 1040 BF Mario-disappearance arc. Peach is alive in it: Luigi is carrying a handkerchief she gave him the week before the brothers left, which places the account beside the existing Luigi's Mansion record at approximately 872 BF. Alice's relationship to that earlier haunting is unresolved and is not asserted here.

What the transcript records is an interrupted rescue that turns out to have three separate operations running through the same building on the same night, none of which knew about the others. Liam entered on a Spirit Residue retrieval that DGK Central Command denies issuing. Mario and Luigi were already inside chasing a string of disappearances. And a two-man crew in modified DGK uniforms crossed the back lawn with a sack while the rest of it was happening.

The account ends in a second-floor study, with Alice's diary reached and never opened.

sections.name: I. Hours of Corridor Before Anybody Spoke
sections.overview:
The flashlight was the only honest thing in the building. Everything else in the Dread Mansion had opinions.

Liam had been walking it for hours by then — long halls that narrowed without turning, floorboards softened under a felt of dust, and a smell somewhere between wet plaster and a closed wardrobe. Things had already come at him in the dark. Some of them had been ghosts. Some of them had been people, which was worse, because the ghosts at least behaved consistently.

He was still alive, and he had stopped counting that as luck.

Then, past a bend in the hall, there were voices. Not the giggling. Voices with words in them.

He followed the sound and found two men holding onto each other under a dead wall sconce. The taller one had a green sweater dusty at the shoulder and both hands full of his brother's jacket.

**"It's really you, Mario! I-it's... it's really you!"**

**"Hahah — of course it's me, Luigi! Who else?"**

The flashlight beam swung across them and stopped. Mario's red cap had slipped sideways. He squinted into the light with his arm still around his brother, and the delight went out of his face by degrees, replaced by something more careful.

**"Another lost one?"**

**"Not lost,"** Liam said. **"I'm here on an assignment. Are you with the DGK too?"**

The brothers exchanged a look. It was not the look of men keeping a secret. It was the look of men who had just been handed a word in a language neither of them spoke.

**"D-DGK? What's that…?"** Luigi said, and pulled his sweater sleeve down over his knuckles.

**"We're not with any group."** Mario scratched under the cap. **"I came here 'cause people were disappearin'. Then Luigi followed me."**

Three men in a corridor, and the only thing any of them could agree on was that the corridor was too long.

Then, from somewhere behind Liam's shoulder, a small delighted giggle came down the hall and did not echo.

*WAH! Note the giggle does not echo. Every other sound in that corridor comes back off the panelling twice — Waluigi has been in enough bad houses to know the acoustics of a long hall. A sound that arrives without a return trip was not made in the corridor. It was made beside his ear.*
sections.imageCaption: The upper corridor as Liam worked it: a dropped torch still burning on the floorboards, dust laid thick enough to hold a bootprint, and no visible end to the hall in either direction.
sections.waluigi_note: Everything in the archive that goes wrong later goes wrong here, in the first thirty seconds, and it goes wrong quietly. Liam names his employer to two strangers. The strangers do not recognise the name. Neither man treats that as information. I have read the transcript four times and nobody in it ever asks the obvious question, which is: if the DGK means nothing to Mario, and Mario has been hunting the disappearances for weeks, who exactly has been briefing Liam? WAH.

sections.name: II. The Visitor Who Was Only Interested in One of Them
sections.overview:
The air changed before anything appeared in it. Breath came out of the three of them in white puffs. The flashlight browned out, recovered, and browned out again.

**"O-oh no! Not again!"** Luigi got behind his brother the way a man gets behind furniture.

Liam pointed the beam down the hall.

She came out of the dark at walking pace without walking. A girl in a Victorian dress gone to rags at the hem, floating a hand's width clear of the boards, lit faintly green from somewhere inside herself. The beam went through her and put a pale coin of light on the wallpaper behind.

**"...Another visitor? How... interesting."**

The voice arrived twice. A young woman's, soft and curious — and under it, half a beat behind, something older that was only using the first voice as a mouth.

**"M-Mario,"** Luigi whispered, far too loudly, **"she's one of *them*!"**

**"One of them?"** Liam said. **"Should I worry?"**

**"Y-yeah! Big worry! All the ghosts here — they're not like normal ones. They're *angry*. They drag people away and—"**

He did not finish, because Alice had stopped tilting her head at Liam.

She was looking at Mario.

*Waluigi has watched a great many things decide who in a room is worth their attention, and they always get it wrong, and they always pick him. This one did not look at the man with the light. It did not look at the man who was frightened. It looked past both of them at the one who had already been introduced.*

Mario stepped forward and put himself across the front of them both, arms slightly out, the way he had presumably done ten thousand times in front of ten thousand worse things.

**"Stay behind me."**

She drifted past his guard as though it were weather. Her hand came up and settled flat on his chest.

His eyes went green. One heartbeat, no longer — the blue came back like a lamp recovering.

But his shoulders came down. His arms lowered. The protective stance simply stopped being held, the way a rope stops being pulled.

And Alice smiled. It was not a predator's smile. It was worse than that: it was fond, and it was sad, and it belonged to somebody who had finally found a thing she had put down years ago and never expected to see again.

**"...You came back."**

Luigi's face lost all its colour. He caught Liam's eye and mouthed three words with no sound behind them at all.

*She's taking him.*
sections.imageCaption: Alice in the lower corridor — translucent, green-lit from within, the torn Victorian hem never quite reaching the floor. The archive's first filed likeness.
sections.waluigi_note: The archive has spent eight years arguing about which of Mario's disappearances was the first one. I am going to say the unpopular thing: this scene is not a possession, it is a reunion, and only one of the two people in it remembers the first meeting. She does not attack him. She does not need to. She puts a hand on him and he stops guarding a corridor he was guarding a second earlier. Whatever the diary turns out to say, it is a second copy of something Mario already has.

sections.name: III. The Hand Under the Floor
sections.overview:
Liam got a fistful of Luigi's sleeve and ran.

**"WAH—!"**

Luigi did not argue. Behind them the fond voice went out of Alice and a low wail came up in its place, moving through the corridors the way wind moves under a door — no direction to it, and no way to shut it out.

**"N-not that way! It leads to the basement! The basement is worse!"**

There was no other way. The house branched wrong. Portraits of nobody in particular watched them go past, and one by one the torches behind them went out, so that the dark closed up at their heels at exactly the speed they were running.

Somewhere ahead, a door slammed on its own.

Then a giggle came from beside Luigi's ear, and Luigi stopped dead.

Liam did not think about it. He drove sideways with his shoulder and took Luigi off his feet, and the two of them went down and rolled through the dust like a dropped bundle of laundry.

**"OOF—!"**

Alice went through the air where their heads had been. She came out the other side of it looking mildly put out, the way a cat does when the mouse moves early.

**"Y-you... pushed me?!"**

He had. Liam was already scrambling up.

Then a hand closed around Luigi's ankle from underneath him — from the shadow the floorboards were casting, not from the floorboards — and it was cold enough that Luigi's whole leg locked.

Liam hauled him up by the wrist like a man pulling a rope out of water. **"GO GO GO!"**

Behind them, Alice did not chase.

She raised one finger and snapped it.

*WAH! A finger-snap and the building shuts its own doors in sequence, west to east, like a butler going round at bedtime. Waluigi does not accept 'haunted' as a description of that. Haunting is atmosphere. This was a house taking an instruction, and somebody in it had standing to give one.*

The house answered. A thud, off in the west of the building. Another, nearer. Another. Doors were closing in sequence down the corridor ahead of them, and the sequence was arriving faster than two men could run through it.

**"N-no no no! All exits are—!"**

The last one was heavy oak, and it went into its frame a body's length in front of their faces with a *BANG* that brought dust off the ceiling in a sheet.

Liam squared his shoulder and told Luigi to hit it with him. **"On three. One... two..."**

Luigi's hands were shaking. He closed them into fists anyway.

**"THREE!"**

*CRACK.* The lock did not hold. The door went wide, and cold clean night came into the hall for the first time in what smelled like a decade.

The giggle followed them out.

**"You can run… but he will return to me."**
sections.waluigi_note: Note what she does and does not do. She does not pursue two escaping men down a corridor. She snaps her fingers and closes the building, and when the building fails to hold them she lets them go with a sentence. I would like the record to be honest about what that sentence is. It is not a threat aimed at Liam or Luigi. It is a statement about a third party, delivered to people she has already decided are irrelevant. She is not hunting. She is waiting for a return she considers scheduled.

sections.name: IV. A Courtyard That Was Not an Exit
sections.overview:
They came out into a moonlit courtyard hedged in on all sides by overgrown box and dead trees, and Luigi ran until his legs quit and then knelt in the grass and breathed.

Behind them the mansion sat with its broken windows and did not follow.

When he could speak he said the thing first: **"You… saved me. I-I would've been taken if it weren't for you."**

Then his face went from relief to something worse, because he had just worked out the shape of what he had done. He had got out. Mario had not.

**"...Do we go back?"**

**"What do you mean?"**

**"I mean… Mario is still *in there*. With her."** He hugged his own arms. **"I know we got out. And I'm glad we did! But—"** the voice cracked on the middle of the sentence and he pushed through it — **"Mario's my brother. He came here because he wanted to save people, and now *he needs saving*."**

Liam said they should go back, but call for help first.

Luigi shook his head before the sentence had finished. No signal — they had checked when they first got lost. The town was hours away on foot, longer if you did not know the roads. And there was the other thing, said flatly, as if it had stopped being surprising a while ago:

**"...And who would come anyway? The police never respond to this mansion. People say it's cursed."**

Liam checked the phone himself, because a man will always check the phone himself.

No bars. Not one dot. Seventeen percent battery, a dark screen, and two exhausted faces reflected in it under the moon.

He read the contact list out into the courtyard anyway, one name at a time, because it was the only list either of them had.

**"John…?"** — No.

**"Sarah?"** — Never heard of her.

**"Mark? Tom? Emily?"** — No, no, and no.

He read the last three the way you read the bottom of a list you have stopped expecting anything from, and Luigi leaned in and gave each of them the same honest, squinting consideration he had given the first five.

**"...Kevin. Jamie. Daniel."**

Nothing.

**"I've only ever known people from Toad Town,"** he said, **"or maybe some Mario fans we meet during races."**

Eight names, read aloud in a dead garden, to a man who could not confirm that any of them existed.

*WAH! Eight names and not one of them lands. Waluigi has audited payrolls that read exactly like this — John, Sarah, Mark, the entire cast of a form somebody filled in quickly. It proves nothing on its own. It proves a great deal in the company of a Central Command that has never heard of the assignment.*
sections.imageCaption: The courtyard, taken from the broken oak door: dead hedge, dead grass, and the mansion's spires standing over the only ground the two of them had managed to reach.
sections.waluigi_note: The roll call is the single most useful three minutes in the transcript and everybody involved treated it as small talk. Eight contacts. One local witness. Zero matches. That is not proof the eight are fictional — Luigi has met perhaps four hundred people in his life and three hundred of them were Toads — but it is the first time anybody holds Liam's employer up to an independent light, and the light goes straight through it.

sections.name: V. The Line That Answered on the Second Try
sections.overview:
He found it near the bottom of the list. **DGK HQ.** *DGK Central — Emergency Line.*

It rang twice and gave him a recording, brisk and corporate and entirely useless: the DGK was offline for maintenance, all agents were advised to check their comms devices regularly, and if this was an emergency — a pause with nothing behind it — please try again later.

The line went dead.

**"Wait — it dialled!"**

It had. Whatever the mansion did to signals, it had not done it to that number. He redialled.

Same two rings. Same recording. But this time, at the very end, after the message had finished and before the silence closed, there was a small mechanical *click* — and then a voice that had not been there the first time.

***"…if you're hearing this and need help — say your name and location."***

**"They can hear us?! Maybe?!"**

**"Uhh — this is Liam. Remember the mission? The one DGK sent me on, to collect samples?"** A half-second of nothing. **"Well guess what — I did it. I got them."**

The silence after that lasted long enough for Luigi to bite his lip.

*Click.*

***"Liam? You're alive?"***

A man. Not a recording. Relieved, and audibly tired.

***"Okay… okay. We thought you were lost. No signal for days."*** Then, sharper: ***"Liam — where are you? Your last tracker ping was near that cursed mansion three hours ago."***

Luigi's head came up at *cursed mansion*. They knew about the building. They knew it by that name.

***"Are samples secure? And… are there others with you?"***

Liam reached into his coat and brought the thing out to show Luigi: a sealed glass vial, and inside it a green liquid that moved when nothing had moved it, turning over on itself slowly like something breathing in its sleep.

**"Yeah. I've got one sample right here."**

The line went quiet in a completely different way.

***"Liam… put that sample down."*** All the warmth had gone out of it. ***"Now."***

***"That liquid isn't supposed to exist outside containment Level 4."***

**"I was told to get it, though?"**

***"Who told you to collect that?"***

The man on the line was not surprised. He was appalled, and those are not the same sound.

***"That glowing green liquid? It's Spirit Residue. Extracted from vengeful spirits — like ghosts or cursed souls who died violently."*** A beat. ***"It only forms where people vanish mysteriously. Places like *that mansion*. Where did YOU get it?!"***

**"Huh — what do you mean? The mission. Right? You told me."**

***"Liam."*** The name, said slowly, the way you say a name when you are testing which side of a lie the person is standing on. ***"I never gave you a mission to collect samples."***

Luigi's jaw came open. Liam heard himself say **"wait, what…"** in a voice that belonged to somebody younger.

***"Who contacted YOU about this mission?"***

Somebody had said DGK. Somebody had said samples. The only organisation that could confirm it [[prop:prop_dgk_retrieval_order|had a file open on him and no order in it]].

*Waluigi would like the reader to sit with the sentence 'I never gave you a mission to collect samples' for a moment longer than Liam did. Liam heard an error. It was not an error. It was the first true thing anybody had said to him in about six weeks, and he spent it on the word 'huh'.*

And then, from beyond the hedge, quite unhurried, somebody began to clap.
sections.waluigi_note: Three separate facts arrive in ninety seconds and the archive has never sorted them properly, so I will. One: the emergency line works from inside a building where nothing else does. Two: the operator knows Liam's name, his tracker, and the containment class of a liquid he should never have seen. Three: the same operator denies the order. Whoever built this did not forge a mission. They forged a *sender* — and left every other part of the DGK working perfectly, because a lure that fails its own security check is not a lure.

sections.name: VI. The Badge Came Out of the Bushes
sections.overview:
He came through the hedge without hurrying. Black coat, silver trim on the edges, hands in his pockets, and a smirk that had been on his face before he arrived and was in no danger of leaving it. The moon found a sharp jaw and a pair of grey eyes with nothing behind them at all.

**"H-Hey!"** Luigi went a step backwards and took Liam's sleeve with him.

**"Who is that?"** Liam said, holding the phone up between them like a small bright shield.

The man stopped a few feet short. He looked at the live call, then at Liam, and he was not surprised by either.

**"You must be Liam."**

Then he leaned very slightly towards the handset. **"Hello? DGK?"**

The line went silent, and then hard. ***"Who are you?"***

He reached into the coat. Luigi made a small noise. What came out was not a weapon; it was [[prop:prop_vale_clearance_badge|a silver badge, held up to the phone like a passport at a border]] — a circle of three intertwined arrows and, around it, DIRECTORATE GLOBAL OPERATIONS · CLEARANCE LEVEL 5.

The pause on the other end of that line is the loudest thing in the transcript.

***"…Director Vale?"***

Respect. Actual respect, from a man who had been giving orders forty seconds earlier.

Vale nodded at the phone as though it could see him, and let the smirk settle into something more professional and considerably worse.

He took another step. Boots in dry leaves.

**"I called *you* here."**

Luigi flinched as if he had been slapped.

Then Vale put out his hand — slowly, giving Liam every opportunity to understand what was about to happen and no opportunity to prevent it — and took the phone out of his fingers.

***"Vale… don't."***

He lifted it to his ear and listened for a moment, the way a man listens to a subordinate he intends to overrule.

**"This operation is now under my direct command."**

***"Director Vale… this mission was never authorized by Central Command."***

**"It is now."**

A beat.

**"All agents involved will stand down or face disciplinary action. This includes you."**

Luigi caught Liam's eye over the top of the black coat and gave him the smallest nod a human neck can produce.

*WAH! Watch the hand. He does not snatch the phone, he reaches for it slowly, in full view, and takes it — because a thing taken slowly from a man who lets you is worth more than a thing grabbed. Waluigi has run this exact confiscation on Wario's accountant. It works on anybody who is still deciding whether to be polite.*

*Run.*
sections.imageCaption: Director Vale on Liam's confiscated phone in the courtyard, mansion behind him. Clearance Level 5, black coat, silver trim, and an operation Central Command had denied ninety seconds earlier.
sections.waluigi_note: I want it on the record that Vale never claims the order was authorised. He says it *is now*, present tense, which is a man converting a denial into a permission by talking over it. The badge is genuine enough to make a Central Command operator change his voice mid-sentence. That is the part that should frighten the reader: not a forged credential, but a real one, in the hands of somebody running an operation his own house says does not exist.

sections.name: VII. Peach's Handkerchief
sections.overview:
They went for the treeline and the treeline let them through.

The path bent. The trees thinned earlier than trees should. And then the ground opened out and there were the tall iron gates, slightly ajar, rusted chain hanging off one of them like something left over from a hanging.

The property had put them back.

**"We're going BACK?!"**

There was no time to answer it and no answer to give. Liam said the only thing that made the situation survivable: **"Well, I guess the only way OUT was through him. And we need to get Mario back, right?"**

Luigi's fists came up and closed. For once his face did something other than fear.

Liam took the vial out of his pocket. It was warm from being carried against his body, and the green in it turned over slowly.

**"W-wait—!"** Luigi's hand came halfway to it and stopped, because he did not have a better idea yet and he knew it. Smashing it here bought nothing. Getting cornered with it in a pocket bought less than nothing — Vale had taken the phone out of Liam's hand without breaking stride, and he would take this the same way.

Then Luigi reached into his overalls and brought out a handkerchief.

Clean white cloth. Small pink flowers embroidered along one edge, close and even, done by somebody who had time.

**"Peach…"**

She had given it to him a week before they left, and she had kissed his cheek and told him to stay safe, and he had carried it since without much using it.

He held it out. Not to take the vial away. To wrap it.

The cloth went round the glass twice and the green light came down to a dull glow through the weave.

They worked out the rest between them in a hedge shadow, in about ninety seconds, and it was the best thinking either of them did all night. Pressure charged the residue — they found that out by accident, by setting the wrapped bundle on the flagstones and putting a boot on it. Push, and the green came up through the linen strong enough to light the underside of a chin. Push harder and it would go.

So they pushed it to just short of that, and stopped, and lifted the boot.

The bundle stayed warm and stayed lit, pulsing slow, like something with a heartbeat wrapped in a napkin.

*WAH! Waluigi has personally been present for four separate attempts to weaponise something nobody understood, and three of them ended with a stretcher. These two did it in a hedge, in ninety seconds, by standing on it carefully. Waluigi refuses to call that luck twice in the same filing, so he will call it once and move on.*

**"Do it,"** Luigi had said, before it worked. Afterwards he did not say anything at all, and carried it in two hands.
sections.waluigi_note: A princess's keepsake became ordnance in under two minutes and nobody in that hedge remarked on it. I am remarking on it. Luigi did not offer the handkerchief because it was cloth; there was a dust sheet on every stick of furniture in that house. He offered the one soft thing he owned that somebody had given him on purpose. Then he pinned it under a boot until it glowed. That is the whole man in one gesture and I would like it filed as such.

sections.name: VIII. The Piano, and What Came Through the Double Doors
sections.overview:
The lower hall was the biggest room in the building and it had been furnished for a life that had stopped. Sheeted chairs stood about in the dark in ones and twos like a congregation nobody had dismissed. Oil paintings hung crooked — some of them serious men from a century ago under a film of grime, some of them nothing at all, just blank primed canvas in a good frame. A grand staircase went up at one end. Heavy double doors stood slightly ajar at the other. Between them ran a frayed rug, and above it two chandeliers with no candles left in their arms, glass fingers curled downward.

Liam pointed at the dust-sheeted grand piano near the wall. Big, solid, and off-centre enough to sit between a man and the doors.

They got behind it and went low.

Silence, then. Liam's own breathing, and the faint hum of a wrapped vial that had been asked to hold a charge.

*Click.*

The double doors swung, slow and deliberate, and moonlight came across the boards in a widening wedge.

Vale walked in.

His coat was still immaculate. His boots crossed the rug at a stroll. He looked around the hall the way you look around a room you have already decided cannot hide anybody indefinitely — no hurry, no anger, a man checking his own arithmetic.

He came level with the middle of the rug.

Luigi's fingers tightened on Liam's arm.

Liam came up over the piano and threw.

The bundle went end over end through the moonlight and struck the boards a stride short of Vale's feet, and the linen let go.

There was no bang. There was a *pulse* — a wide flat wash of green that went out across the floor and up the walls and made every sheet in the room grey-white for half a second — and it hit Vale in the chest like an open hand. His coat flared. He went down onto one knee with his head lowered and both palms flat on the rug, and for the first time that night, nothing about him was smug.

Luigi did not wait to be told. He came out from behind the piano, took a heavy candlestick off a side table two-handed, and brought it down.

Not on the head. On the shoulder.

***CRACK.***

Vale grunted, went over sideways, and stopped moving.

For about four seconds, the plan had worked completely.

*Waluigi wishes to congratulate the green sweater. Not the throw — the throw was fine — the candlestick. Aimed at the shoulder, which puts a man down, and not at the head, which puts a man in the ground and a witness in a cell. That is a frightened person making a correct decision at speed, and it is rarer than courage.*
sections.imageCaption: The lower hall after the throw: the sheeted grand they had hidden behind, the frayed rug, and the shattered vial still burning green on the boards.
sections.waluigi_note: Four seconds. I have counted them off the transcript and four is generous. In that window the party held every piece: the sample was spent but spent *usefully*, the ranking hostile was face-down on his own rug, and the staircase to the second floor was unguarded. Everything that happens afterwards happens because nobody in the room had planned past the good outcome. Write that on the inside of your helmet. The dangerous part of a plan that works is the second after it works.

sections.name: IX. The Man Who Was Already Him
sections.overview:
Something hit Liam from behind in the small of the back and took him off his feet.

It was not Luigi. Luigi was eight feet away with a candlestick in his hands and his mouth open.

Arms came round Liam's chest like a pair of iron bands and put him on the floor hard enough to empty his lungs. He got his head up.

He was standing over himself.

Same jacket. Same haircut. The same pale astonished expression that must have been on his own face at that exact moment, worn by somebody else at the same time, so that for one bad instant the only way to tell them apart was which of them was on the boards.

**"LIAM?!"**

Luigi took a step and stopped, because there was no correct direction for the step to go in.

Liam's hand went to his pocket and closed on the folding knife he had forgotten he was carrying. He snapped it open and got it up between them.

The copy did not flinch. The copy smiled — a wide, patient, entirely wrong smile that Liam had certainly never made with his own mouth — and produced its own knife. Identical. Same size, same handle, same small nick out of the bolster.

Metal met metal and stayed there, both arms shaking, the piano strings humming faintly under the pressure a few feet away.

And then the fight moved without either of them moving.

Liam had been underneath. He blinked, and he was standing, and the duplicate was on the boards beneath him — same position, same knife-lock, roles exactly reversed, no interval in between and no memory of getting up. Not thrown. Not rolled. *Swapped*, the way a card is swapped, and the copy grinned up at him from the floor as though it had been expecting the trick and had been waiting to see how he took it.

Luigi looked from one of them to the other and back, and could not tell.

Behind them, Vale groaned and moved one arm.

*WAH! Waluigi has been impersonated by a mirror, a fey, a poster, and once by Wario in a wig, and none of them could do this. The face is theatre. Trading places mid-lock is the actual attack, and it means the thing in that hall was not copying Liam. It was sharing his position in the room and choosing which half to be.*
sections.imageCaption: The stand-off in the lower hall. Two identical men, one of them tense and one of them wearing an expression the other has never made.
sections.waluigi_note: I have read plenty of shapeshifter filings and they all get one thing wrong, which is that they treat the face as the weapon. The face was not the weapon here. The position swap was. A duplicate that merely looks like you can be sorted out by a friend with a good memory and thirty seconds; a duplicate that can trade places with you mid-grapple cannot be sorted out by anybody, ever, including you. Luigi froze because freezing was correct. There was no honest way for him to help.

sections.name: X. The Floorboard, and Three Options Nobody Liked
sections.overview:
The copy came on again. It never stood still and it never hurried; the knife stayed low and its eyes stayed on Liam's hands, not his face.

Liam gave ground, and the board under his heel creaked, and then split.

One edge dropped an inch. His ankle went over sideways — not broken, but done taking his weight — and the whole hall went quiet enough that Vale twitched at the noise.

The copy lunged, knife coming down.

Luigi abandoned Vale entirely and dived, and took the duplicate across the ribs with his shoulder at full length. The blade missed Liam's chest by inches and went into the boards to the handle, standing up out of the floor like a small flag.

Then everybody was on the ground and nobody had won anything. Vale was groaning properly now. The copy put a boot on the boards, pulled its knife free, and turned around.

Liam laid it out fast, because there was no time to lay it out well. Three options.

**"One — you fight Vale, I'll fight the doppelgänger. Two — we fight the doppelgänger together and risk Vale getting up. Three — we run."** A breath. **"I think... any better ideas?"**

Luigi held up three fingers and, for the second time that night, was better at this than anybody expected.

**One.** Throw something across the hall. Break a vase, shout from a doorway. Let the copy chase the noise, and go for Mario while it does.

**Two.** Leave Vale to it. Vale was already waking up in a room with a supernatural intruder in it, and Vale had spent the whole night behaving as though everything in this building was his to command. Let him find out.

**Three.** Find Alice's diary.

**"Alice's diary? I've never heard of that."**

Luigi's voice dropped to almost nothing.

**"Mario found it. On the second floor. There was a woman named Alice — a spirit, she died here years ago."** She had loved Riba, the man who owned the mansion. Riba betrayed her. She died, and what she left behind of herself went into the house.

**"Why would she possess Mario?"**

**"Because… Mario was the first person who found her diary."**

He read it. He read about her pain and her love and what was done to her, and — Luigi said this part like a man confessing to something on his brother's behalf — Mario had *felt sorry for her*. That was the door. Not a curse, not a trap. Compassion, offered to something that had been alone in a building for a very long time and had stopped being kind a long way back.

*WAH! So the trap is pity. Not a curse, not a cursed object, not a rune anybody could have spotted — a diary left where a decent man would find it, and the only key required is being sorry for the person who wrote it. Waluigi is, for once, entirely serious: that is the most dangerous door in this archive.*

**"So instead of thanking Mario… she possessed him."**

The diary was the only option with an object attached to it.

Liam chose the diary, and left two dangers in one room in the hope that they preferred each other's company.
sections.waluigi_note: Luigi's three ideas were better than Liam's three, and Luigi produced them while bleeding adrenaline on a floor next to a man who could swap places with reality. The archive has him filed as the frightened brother for eighty years and it has never once revised the entry. He proposed misdirection, then a controlled collision between two enemies, then the retrieval of the only object anybody had a reason to want. Under fire. On his knees. I would take him over most captains I have worked with. WAH.

sections.name: XI. The Study with the Cracked Blue Handle
sections.overview:
They took the stairs. Behind them came one heavy impact, the sound of a blade going into something that was not a person, and Vale's first genuinely angry shout of the night. Luigi did not look back and Liam did not ask him to.

The second-floor corridor was narrower and colder than the hall below, and it had been papered a long time ago in something with a pattern that had given up. The paper hung off the walls in tongues. Crooked portraits went down both sides with the faces blurred out under dust.

Luigi pointed left without stopping. **"There."**

The door at the end of the narrow hall stood slightly open, moonlight coming through the fanlight above it, and the handle was cracked blue porcelain — which was how Mario had described it, which was how Luigi knew.

Inside, the study had been abandoned mid-thought. A big wooden desk in the centre with papers gone soft and ink pots gone solid. A shattered oil lamp lying on its side where somebody had knocked it over leaving in a hurry. Two walls of shelves, mostly empty, the rest holding books that had grown into their own bindings. One window cracked open a finger's width, and through it a bar of moonlight that laid the dust out in the air like slow rain.

And on the corner of the desk, exactly where a man might set something down and mean to come back for it: a small leather-bound book. The cover worn pale at the corners. The pages frayed.

Alice's diary.

There was no glow. Nothing floated. It sat there being a book. But the air in that corner of the room was heavier than the air by the door, in the way that a held breath is heavier than a taken one, and both of them noticed it and neither of them said so.

Luigi hung back. He had a specific reluctance about it — not fear of the room but a scruple about the object, the way a decent person hesitates over reading somebody else's letters even when the somebody is dead and hunting his brother.

Vale would be up soon. The copy might already be finished downstairs.

He looked at Liam, waiting to be told it was all right.

*Waluigi notes that the room is described in full — the ink gone solid, the lamp on its side, the dust hanging in the moonbar — and that the book gets three lines. That is the transcript telling on itself. Everybody in that study was looking hard at the furniture because nobody wanted to be first to touch the diary.*
sections.waluigi_note: Nobody opens it. That is the fact the whole file turns on and I will not let a later archivist smooth it over: the diary is reached, and looked at, and never read, because Liam glanced sideways at that moment and saw a corner of paper in his companion's pocket. An entire chain of consequence in this archive exists because a man was distracted from the correct object by a smaller one at exactly the wrong second. The book is still on that desk as far as anybody here knows.

sections.name: XII. A Note Folded Since Yesterday
sections.overview:
There was something sticking out of Luigi's pocket. Yellowed at the edges, folded twice, carried long enough to go soft at the creases.

**"Are you hiding more?"**

Luigi froze, and that was answer enough.

The handwriting was large and cheerfully bad, and it went like this:

> *"Oh, hi there Mario! I hope you don't mind, but I had to take all of those power stars and seal them all away in those paintings. I also had to kidnap the princess again… you know the routine, big bad guy and all, haha! Anyway, try to collect them all and fight me so we can see who wins! Then we can go get some ice cream at the place I told you about! See you then, buddy!"*
>
> **— Bowser**

Two sentences into it, Liam stopped being confused about the blank canvases in the hall downstairs. Paintings. Sealed away in *those paintings* — and a whole lower hall of frames with nothing painted in them, hung at eye level in a house where people came in and did not come out.

And a fifth of the way down the same note, in the same friendly hand, between a boast and an offer of ice cream: *I also had to kidnap the princess again.*

Luigi had gone the colour of the wallpaper.

**"How long have you had that?"**

**"...Since yesterday."**

It had been handed to him at a checkpoint near the mansion's outer gate. A Koopa guard had put it into his hand, said **"For you,"** and given no reason. He had read it standing there, and then folded it twice and said nothing to anybody, including his brother, for a day and a night.

**"You didn't read it until now. Why?"**

**"I… I was scared."**

He said it quietly and did not dress it up. Mario had been right next to him. They were three hours into looking for people who had gone missing in a haunted house. If Luigi had held that paper up, Mario would have dropped Alice's case where it stood and run for Peach, because Mario has never in his life prioritised correctly under that particular pressure. So [[prop:prop_bowser_painting_note|the note stayed folded]], and the brothers stayed on the case, and eleven hours later Alice put her hand on Mario's chest.

And then, because the room had gone quiet and Liam had asked, Luigi told the rest of it.

Mario came because people were vanishing near the property — folks who went out at night and did not come back. He came alone, because of course he did. Luigi followed when Mario stopped coming back either. The front gate had been unlocked. Inside there had been no staff, no guards, no dogs: an expensive house standing perfectly still and going soft in the middle.

They found the diary in the study. Mario read it. After that his eyes went green sometimes, and he began talking about punishing Riba — repeatedly, urgently, and at length, about a man who has been dead for the better part of a century.

Boos came through the walls after that. And once, while Alice had him, Mario had turned and looked directly at the vial in Liam's coat before anybody had mentioned it was there.

There was one more thing, and Luigi produced it reluctantly because he had spent a week deciding it was nerves. Before any of it — before the diary, before the green — he had seen a woman standing at the garden gate at night. Pale. Dark hair. A dress a century out of fashion.

She had not done anything. She had watched them go in.

*WAH! A woman at the gate, watching two men walk in, doing nothing. Waluigi will say what Luigi spent a week not saying: she was not haunting the garden. She was checking the arrivals. Something in that house wanted to know who was coming before it decided what to be.*
sections.waluigi_note: File the note as a delivery, not a taunt. A Koopa guard stood at a checkpoint on the road to this specific mansion and handed Bowser's paper to the specific brother most likely to sit on it. The archive is entitled to ask why the Koopa Troop had a man on that road at all. And I will say the quiet part: two separate operations were converging on that house the same week, one of them hiding Power Stars in paintings, one of them extracting Spirit Residue, and neither has ever been shown to know about the other.

sections.name: XIII. Two Figures, One Sack
sections.overview:
**"Is there a window in here?"**

There was — small, maybe two feet by three, old wooden frame that complained when Luigi put a hand on it, one pane cracked but clear. Beyond it the moonlit gardens went away into hedges and a broken fountain and, past all of that, the dark.

Liam looked down, and there were two figures crossing the lawn.

Purple and yellow. One short and wide with a crooked nose, one tall and lean with a stride like a pair of scissors. Both of them in what were unmistakably DGK uniforms and equally unmistakably not DGK uniforms — the black cut about and re-tailored, patches slapped onto clothes that had never been part of any issue, the whole effect of a costume assembled by somebody who had seen one from a distance.

The short one was dragging a sack. It was enormous, roped shut, and bulging in ways that suggested corners.

**"It's like Santa,"** Liam said. **"Look at that big sack."**

Luigi leaned into the glass. **"...Are they working for Vale?"**

**"Probably not? But they have the uniforms, right? I've never seen those two."**

Luigi frowned, because the answer was no, and the reason was obvious once he had looked properly. Real DGK men were sleek and black and silver-marked. These two moved wrong. No discipline in it at all — hurrying, glancing about, the tall one checking behind them every eight paces. Not agents. Not even good thieves. Two men playing soldier with a haul they had not earned, heading for the back gate at the speed of people who have heard a noise indoors.

They went through it and away down the dirt path that runs out through the trees to the road, and the gate swung behind them and kept swinging.

*WAH! Waluigi is aware of how this looks and declines to improve it. Yes, that is his uniform. No, it is not a real one — Wario sewed the patches on in a hotel room and cut the shoulders wrong, and Waluigi walked around a haunted property all night looking like a lampshade with a rank.*

And Liam, watching an empty lawn, replayed the last thirty seconds and took one step backwards.

**"Wait. You know what DGK is."** The words came out flat. **"You said you didn't. Before."**

Luigi turned round with his hands half up.

He had. Nobody had told him the name. Liam had said the letters once, hours ago in a corridor, and got a blank look for it, and now Luigi had used the word himself, correctly, about a uniform, in a sentence nobody had prompted.

His mouth opened and nothing came out of it.

Then, small: **"I... I saw the uniform before."**
sections.waluigi_note: I was in the garden. I am filing this record and I was thirty feet below that window with a rope-handle in my fist, and I did not know until years afterwards that anyone was watching. So: the uniforms were modified because Wario modified them, badly, with a needle, in a hotel room, and the sack was full and I am not itemising it here. What I will confirm is the important part — nobody sent us. We were not Vale's. Two operations in one house that night, and the second one was just us. WAH.

sections.name: XIV. To My Brave Boys
sections.overview:
**"Did you lie to me? Can I really trust you?"**

**"No! I didn't lie on purpose!"**

The panic in it was real, and so was the desperation to be believed, and neither of those is evidence of anything, and Liam knew it.

The explanation came out in a rush. Days ago, while Mario was already missing, a DGK patrol had passed near the house they were staying in — men in black, searching for something, not asking anyone anything. Luigi had stayed inside and listened through a window and heard two words he did not understand and had not been able to put down since: *containment*, and *enforcement*.

That was all of it. He had never met one. He had never spoken to one. He had heard a word through a window and it had frightened him, and hours ago in a dark corridor a stranger had said the same letters at him and he had not connected the two until he saw the uniforms on the lawn.

It was, Liam had to admit, exactly as convincing as the truth usually is, which is to say not very.

**"I swear on Mario's life… I'm not working with them."**

Liam did not answer.

The silence went on. Luigi did not fill it and did not beg, which was somehow worse; he just stood there with his hands open and let himself be looked at.

Then he reached into his pocket again — slowly, telegraphing every part of the movement — and what came out was not paper.

It was a photograph, worn white along the folds, carried for years.

Two boys in front of a small house. The taller one perhaps ten, one arm already slung protectively round the smaller one's shoulders, both of them in identical red-and-blue striped shirts that had obviously been made at home by the same pair of hands. The smaller one already had the green cap on.

**"What is this?"**

**"That's us… when we were kids."**

Liam turned it over.

On the back, in faded ink, in handwriting that belonged to neither of them:

> ***"To my brave boys. Always protect each other."***

No names. No date. Nothing to prove whose hand it was, and nothing needed.

He handed it back without saying anything. Luigi took it in both palms, looked at it for a second, and put it away against his chest.

Outside, the wind moved in the dead trees. Inside, two people who had known each other for about five hours stood in a dusty study with a book neither of them had opened.

**"......we should get Mario and leave....."**

Then Liam pushed the window up and said the reasonable thing, which was the wrong thing: split up. Luigi takes Mario, Liam goes after the two men with the sack.

**"No—!"** Luigi had his arm before the sentence was done, and shook his head hard. Alice was loose. Vale was waking. The copy was somewhere on a staircase. **"We stay together."**

Liam closed the window. It clicked shut, and his breath fogged a small oval on the cracked pane, and the oval shrank and went away.

Step one: find Mario, before she has all of him.

Step two: work out what the diary is for.

Out on the lawn, with nobody left to see it, the back gate was still swinging.

aftermath:
Nothing in this file closed. Mario remained under Alice's influence, in the building, unrecovered. The diary was reached, set on a desk corner, looked at, and never opened — it is presumed still there.

Custody, since the archive keeps losing track of it: the Spirit Residue vial was expended in the lower hall and is gone. Peach's handkerchief was destroyed with it. Liam's phone left with Director Vale and has never been recovered, along with the call log that would identify who actually briefed the retrieval. Bowser's note and the childhood photograph both stayed in Luigi's pocket. The sack that crossed the back lawn was never inventoried.

Standing: DGK Central Command and Director Vale ended the night in open contradiction on a live line, with an operator ordered to stand down by a superior his own house says was running nothing. That dispute is now the case rather than the haunting. Injuries were minor — a turned ankle for Liam, a shoulder Vale will feel for a fortnight, and Luigi's sweater. The mansion's exits still loop, the emergency line still connects from inside it, and both facts remain unexplained.
waluigiAssessment:
Waluigi was on the grounds that night and not in the rooms, and this filing keeps the distinction: the garden beat is his own testimony and the interior scenes are reconstructed from the account. He is not going to claim a corridor he was not standing in.

**One. The mission was not forged. The sender was.** Every other part of the DGK worked correctly all night — the emergency line connected from inside a building where nothing else did, the operator had Liam's tracker history, and he named the containment class of the liquid on sight. A fabricated organisation does not pass its own security check. Somebody with real access inserted a real-looking order into a real system, and the only object that could name them left the property in Vale's coat pocket.

**Two. Vale never actually claimed authorisation.** Read the exchange again. Central says the mission was never authorised; he answers *"It is now."* Present tense. That is not a man producing a permission, it is a man converting a denial into one by outranking the person holding it. His badge is genuine enough to change a Central operator's voice mid-sentence, and that should worry the reader considerably more than a forgery would.

**Three. Alice was not hunting.** She closed the house, let two men out of it, and spent her only sentence on a third party who was not present: *"He will return to me."* She recognised Mario before either brother could establish how. Whatever the diary contains, she is working from a copy she already had.

**Four. The door was pity, and pity is not detectable.** Mario was not cursed, tricked, or ambushed. He read a dead woman's account of what was done to her, and he was sorry for her, and that was the whole key. There is no ward against a decent reaction. File that under things this archive cannot issue a countermeasure for.

**Five. The duplicate's weapon was the position swap, not the face.** A copy of a man can be sorted out by a friend with a good memory. A thing that trades places with him mid-grapple cannot be sorted out by anybody, including the man. Luigi froze because freezing was the only honest option available to him.

**Recommendation: go back for the book.** Not for Alice, not for Vale, not for the sack — for the diary, which is on a desk in a second-floor study behind a cracked blue handle, and which is the only object in this file that anybody has a reason to want. Everything else in the record is people arguing about who is allowed to be in the building. WAH.

name: The Siege of Shadow Pass
title: A Desperate Stand in the Ruins of Gondorian Fortifications: The Siege of Shadow Pass, 1028 BF
era: During the early years of Mordor's ascension as a dominant force in Middle-earth
location: Ruins of Shadow Pass, within the borders of Mordor
summary: A small contingent of Gondorian defenders held out against a numerically superior Mordorian force at the crumbling Ruins of Shadow Pass, delaying their advance into the heartland of Gondor for several weeks.
description:
## Prologue:

The Gathering Storm The sun hung low in the sky, its final rays casting long shadows across the barren landscape that led to Shadow Pass. The air was thick with the scent of ash and smoke, a reminder of the fires that had ravaged the land just days ago. From afar, the crumbling ruins seemed like skeletal fingers reaching toward the heavens, their stone bones gnarled and twisted by the elements. The wind whispered through the gaps between the stones, carrying with it the distant sound of war horns and the clatter of armor. To the north, a small contingent of Gondorian soldiers could be seen, though their numbers were few.

They moved slowly, each step careful to avoid the loose gravel that threatened to trip them.

Their eyes, accustomed to the dim light filtering through the ruins, darted around, searching for any sign of approaching Mordor's forces.

The soldiers wore a patchwork of armor, some pieces old and rusted, others newly polished but far from perfect.

The ground beneath their feet was uneven, littered with debris from the recent battle.

Broken spears, shattered shields, and remnants of cloth banners lay scattered about, telling stories of valiant struggles long past.

The air hummed with tension, a palpable force that seemed to press against every man's skin, making each breath harder to take.

The distant sound of hoof beats echoed ominously in the distance, a reminder that their time was running out.

A young scout, no more than sixteen summers old, crouched behind a large stone slab.

His eyes scanned the horizon, searching for any sign of Mordor's advance.

He held his breath as he listened intently to the sounds around him—his heart pounding in his chest like the war drums that had long ago begun their ominous roll.

Every movement was deliberate, every glance sharp and focused.

For behind these ruins, a gathering storm brewed, one that would soon test the courage of those who chose to remain.

## The Siege Unfolds


The Siege Unfolds The air was thick with tension as the Mordorian army slowly encircled the crumbling Ruins of Shadow Pass. The defenders, a motley crew from various corners of Gondor—some with beards worn to stubble, others still sporting the livery of distant provinces—huddled behind hastily constructed barricades. Dust and stone crumbled under the relentless pounding of Mordorian catapults; each missile sent fragments dancing through the air like desolate snowflakes. The defenders’ eyes were fixed on the horizon, where the sun dipped lower, casting long shadows that stretched across the battlefield.

The wind carried a faint whisper of autumn—dry and crisp, but there was no respite from the heat.

Sweat mingled with dirt on their skin, creating a sticky layer that made every movement labored.

Among them stood a soldier named Elion, whose homeland lay far to the east in Anfalas.

His sword, though battered by countless battles, still gleamed in the fading light.

He listened intently as the Mordorians’ war cries echoed across the valley, sharp and menacing like the cawing of crows at dusk.

The ground trembled beneath his boots with each impact of their battering rams against the walls.

Elion turned to a younger recruit, still fresh from the hills of Lamedon. "Hold firm," he said quietly.

The boy nodded, though his hands trembled slightly.

Nearby, the healers moved among them, tending wounds and offering words of encouragement.

Their eyes, too, were filled with resolve, their voices steady but laden with a quiet desperation.

The Mordorian commander, known only as Black Stone, stood atop a nearby hill, surveying the scene with a cold, calculating gaze.

His soldiers, though numerous, showed no signs of hastening their assault; they moved with the precision of predators closing in on their prey.

The rumble of war machines continued unceasingly, and the defenders’ resolve seemed to grow stronger by the moment.

As night fell, casting an eerie glow from the torches set up by both sides, the sounds of battle grew more distant, replaced by the hushed whispers of those who remained vigilant.

The stars above twinkled faintly, offering little solace in the ever-intensifying struggle.

Inside the ruins, the defenders prepared for another day of conflict, knowing that every moment they held out was a victory against the looming shadow of Mordor itself.

## Allies and Enemies


The air outside Shadow Pass was thick with the stench of burning wood and the acrid smell of roasted earth. The Gondorian defenders, huddled within the crumbling ruins, could hear the distant sounds of Mordor’s army moving ever closer. The ground trembled under the weight of unseen forces, and every shadow seemed to carry a hint of the Dark Lord's will. Among them stood Eliran, a young ranger with eyes as sharp as any in Gondor. His tunic was torn, and his hands were calloused from constant labor. He moved silently through the ruins, checking on supplies and ensuring that the men and women inside the fortifications were prepared for another day of conflict.

The sounds of distant drums and horns echoed like a funeral march, each beat echoing in Eliran’s chest.

From a distance, Elenwen, a healer from Minas Tirith, could be seen tending to her wounded comrades.

Her hands moved with practiced precision as she applied poultices and set broken bones.

The air around her was heavy with the smell of herbs and the faint scent of blood.

She worked tirelessly, her face illuminated only by the flickering light of torches that barely held back the encroaching darkness.

Farther down the crumbling walls stood Aelir, a former blacksmith who had taken up arms against his will.

His hands were rough from years of labor and now raw from the constant strain of holding a sword.

He moved with a quiet desperation, checking for any weak points in the defenses that could be exploited by Mordor’s forces.

Outside, the Mordorian ranks stretched as far as the eye could see.

Their armor glinted under the pale light of an almost-full moon, and their voices were a low hum of anticipation.

Among them was Vargor, a captain from the northern reaches of Mordor.

His skin was darkened by years of sun and wind, and his eyes gleamed with a cold determination.

He knew that this would be the key to breaking Gondor’s defenses, but the defenders inside held fast.

The night was long, filled with the sounds of distant clashes and the occasional scream of pain.

Inside the ruins, Eliran could hear the soft murmurings of his comrades as they prepared for another day of conflict.

Every moment they held out was a victory against the looming shadow of Mordor itself.

## Echoes of the Past Eliran shivered as a cold gust swept through the crumbling walls of Shadow Pass.


The air was thick with dust and the scent of decay, mingling with the faint tang of sulfur that hinted at Mordor's proximity. His fingers traced the jagged stones that had once been part of the fortifications, now weathered to the point where they crumbled under his touch. Each grain of sand he brushed aside felt like a reminder of the countless battles fought here. In the distance, the silhouette of Mordor loomed on the horizon, its dark clouds and jagged peaks casting long shadows that seemed to stretch towards the defenders. The distant rumble of engines and the occasional explosion from within the siege lines reminded Eliran that they were but a small speck in the vast machinery of war.

Yet, he held his ground, determined not to let this place fall into the hands of the enemy.

Amongst the shadows, whispers carried by the wind spoke of lost heroes and forgotten tales.

The stories told here often involved minor figures like Eliran’s comrades—men and women from distant regions who had joined the cause without fanfare or glory.

There was Taria, a healer whose delicate hands could mend wounds that seemed beyond saving.

Her presence among the defenders was as crucial as any weapon, yet her role was unseen by many.

Then there were the scouts like Eron, whose eyes had seen more than anyone should in a lifetime.

His skin bore the marks of countless scars, each one a silent testament to his valor and endurance.

Despite their grim surroundings, he maintained an unwavering smile that could light up even the darkest corners.

It was said that he could navigate through the ruins blindfolded, knowing every crevice and shadow by heart.

Eliran’s eyes flickered from one figure to another, each a part of this intricate tapestry.

Though their names might not be etched in history books, they were integral to the defense of Shadow Pass.

In their quiet perseverance lay the true strength of Gondor—its people, its resilience, and its unyielding will to defend against all odds.

The murmurings around him grew louder as preparations intensified for another day’s battle, yet Eliran could not help but feel a profound connection to these distant lands and their brave inhabitants.

summary: A curious and somewhat alarming event unfolded when a group of young druids discovered an ancient artifact embedded deep within the roots of a centennial tree. The discovery led to unexplained phenomena that puzzled the local community for weeks.
description:
## Prologue: Echoes from Forgotten Glade

In the heart of the ancient forest, where shadows stretched like forgotten whispers, the druids moved with a quiet grace that only long years of communion with nature could bestow. The air was thick with the scent of pine and damp earth, a fragrance that seemed to hum with secrets from ages past. As twilight approached, casting an eerie glow over the landscape, a small group of young druids, their faces illuminated by the faint light of a half-moon, set out on a journey into the densest part of the forest. The ground beneath them was soft and yielding, a carpet of moss that whispered with every step.

They followed an old path, one barely visible through the thick undergrowth, until they reached a massive tree, its trunk wider than any man could hug.

The roots of this ancient sentinel were covered in lichen, each frond glistening like emerald jewels under the strange moonlight.

It was here that their quest led them.

As they began to dig around the base of the tree, the air grew colder, and a peculiar stillness settled over the glade.

Each tool strike against stone sent vibrations through the ground, a low rumble that seemed to echo from deep within the earth itself.

The druids' eyes widened as they uncovered a smooth, black object buried deep in the roots—an artifact unlike any they had seen before.

Its surface was etched with symbols that shimmered faintly under the moonlight, casting an otherworldly glow.

The discovery did not go unnoticed by all.

Somewhere beyond their sight, in the distant realms of the forest, eyes watched from the shadows.

Elders of forgotten glades, guardians of lore long since lost to time, stirred in their slumber.

They knew of this artifact, though it had lain dormant for centuries.

Now, with its uncovering, a chain of events was set in motion that would ripple through the fabric of the forest’s magic.

The strange moonlight lingered, casting an ethereal light over the glade, and as the druids marveled at their find, they felt a connection to something ancient and powerful.

Yet, in the silence following their discovery, there was also a sense of unease—a reminder that not all knowledge should be revealed.

## Rogue Element and the Moonlight Enigma After days of careful excavation, the druids found themselves face-to-face with an ancient artifact—a silver pendant embedded deep within the roots of a centuries-old tree.


The pendant was unlike any they had ever seen; its surface shimmered under the moonlight, casting strange, shifting shadows that seemed to dance on their skin like living whispers. The air around them grew thick and heavy, as if the very atmosphere held secrets they were not prepared to uncover. One of the younger druids, Elara, felt a chill run down her spine. The pendant pulsed faintly with an energy that was both familiar and alien, stirring old memories she could barely recall. Her hands trembled slightly as she reached out to touch it, and when her fingers brushed its surface, a low hum filled the air, a sound that seemed to resonate within her bones.

As the night wore on, the phenomena grew more pronounced.

Strange lights flickered between the trees, casting an eerie glow over the clearing.

The wind howled through the branches in a rhythm that matched the pulse of the artifact.

The druids stood motionless, their breaths coming in sharp gasps as they tried to comprehend what was happening.

From the shadows emerged figures—ghostly forms with eyes like glowing embers.

These were not ordinary spirits; they moved with purposeful intent, though no sound could be heard from them.

They drifted around the group, their presence felt more than seen, and Elara knew then that she had stumbled upon something far older than any legend.

The pendant’s glow intensified as the moon reached its zenith, bathing everything in a silver light that seemed to seep into the very marrow of the earth.

The druids stood silent, their minds racing with questions they dared not voice aloud.

Were these spirits messengers from some forgotten age? Or was the artifact itself alive, whispering secrets only those who listened could hear? The night passed, and as dawn broke, the strange lights faded, the wind died down, and the pendant’s glow dimmed to a faint sheen.

The druids left the clearing with heavy hearts, each one carrying with them not just the memory of what they had seen but also the weight of a responsibility they did not fully understand.

## Whispers in the Heartland Plains


The whispers in the Heartland Plains began not with words, but with the subtlest of sounds—rustling leaves that seemed to whisper secrets in a language only the wind and the trees could understand. The young druids, fresh from their discovery, felt an eerie calm settle over them as they retraced their steps through the dense forest. The air was thick with the scent of damp earth and pine needles, a smell that clung to their clothes long after they left the clearing. Their path took them past the towering figures of ancient trees, their gnarled roots twisting like the hands of time itself. The light from the half-moon filtered through the canopy above, casting elongated shadows on the forest floor.

Shadows that moved ever so slightly as if they were alive with some unseen force.

The druids' breaths came in short gasps, each one aware of the weight of their responsibility pressing down upon them.

As they ventured further into the heart of the woods, the sounds grew louder—a low hum, like distant thunder, but closer and more insistent.

It seemed to originate from deep within the earth itself.

The ground beneath their feet felt alive, vibrating with an energy that was both familiar and foreign.

They knelt beside a particularly ancient oak, its bark cracked and fissured as if it had seen countless seasons.

Here, they found the artifact—a small, intricate stone carving embedded in the roots.

The druids' fingers trembled slightly as they touched the cold stone.

It was smooth to the touch, yet radiated an inexplicable warmth that seemed to emanate from deep within its core.

Their breaths quickened further as strange symbols began to glow faintly around the artifact.

The ground rumbled beneath them once more, and a low, guttural growl echoed through the forest.

The druids exchanged uneasy glances, their hearts heavy with the realization that they were part of something much larger than themselves.

They knew not what, but the knowledge was there in the air—something ancient stirring from its slumber, awakening to claim its due.

The whispers grew louder as they made their way back through the forest, each step a silent acknowledgment of the weighty responsibility they now carried.

## Epilogue: Peaceful Transition


The forest hummed with a renewed life as they emerged from their journey. The air was thick with the scent of damp earth and decaying leaves, a testament to the ancient cycle that had just been disturbed. Sunlight filtered through the canopy in fractured shafts, casting dappled patterns on the ground below. Their feet crunched softly against the fallen debris—sticks, leaves, and seeds—each step a reminder of the path they had tread. The young druids exchanged quiet looks, their expressions a mix of awe and apprehension. The artifact, now safely within the confines of their sacred grove, seemed to stir with each breath of wind, as if it were alive.

The whispers that had begun in the forest deepened into conversations, carried by the soft hum of nature itself.

Birds sang in unison, a melody that seemed both natural and orchestrated—a reminder that all was not yet at peace.

The villagers, who had been wary of the druids' absence, began to gather outside their huts, curiosity piqued by the mysterious return.

The elders, with their weathered faces and deep-set eyes, met them on the edge of the village square.

Their hands were gnarled, yet they moved with a grace that belied their age.

The druids lowered themselves to the ground in respectful greeting, each one bowing their heads low.

The elders' eyes twinkled with a mixture of wisdom and concern as they listened intently. "It is a heavy burden you bear," said one elder, his voice like the rustling of autumn leaves. "The land speaks through its children now." He paused, letting the weight of those words sink in before continuing. "But do not fear.

The ancient ones have always found their way back to us." The druids nodded, their resolve strengthened by the words of wisdom passed down through generations.

The village square felt smaller, more intimate as the gathering grew.

The community, once divided in its curiosity and fear, now stood united under a sky that seemed both brighter and darker.

As the sun dipped low on the horizon, casting long shadows across the land, the druids began to set up the ceremonial fire.

Flames licked at the night air, a beacon for those who had sought answers throughout the weeks.

The village watched in hushed whispers, knowing that this was but the beginning of their journey—a journey that would test their strength and their unity.

The flames danced higher as the night deepened, illuminating the faces of those gathered.

Each face held a story, each story part of the rich tapestry that made up this community.

The druids' hands moved with purpose, their eyes fixed on the fire, a symbol of the bond they had just rekindled.
